title: How to read a Church document
hookLine: constitutions, encyclicals, exhortations: different weights, all cited by numbered paragraphs
tomorrow: how does a council picture God talking to people?

lines: A LATIN NAME AND A SMALL NUMBER.
HOW DO YOU FIND YOUR WAY?
cards: A homily mentions Lumen Gentium 11. A news story quotes a pope's encyclical, paragraph something. A parish bulletin cites an exhortation.
No page numbers, no chapters: just a Latin name and a small number, as if every copy on earth were the same book.
For the next stretch of days, this path opens the Church's own documents and reads them a few lines at a time. First, the puzzle of how to find your way around one.

teach.b: A constitution is a council's own teaching document, and the bishops of the Second Vatican Council called some of theirs dogmatic constitutions, which marks them as weighty: Dei Verbum, on God's word, and Lumen Gentium, on the Church.
An encyclical is a letter from a pope, addressed to the bishops and often to the whole Church, sometimes to everyone of good will.
An exhortation is often written after a meeting of bishops, gathering up what was said and urging the Church on.
Different kinds, different weights, and Catholic teaching takes those weights seriously. Next, the names.

teach.h: NAMED BY THEIR FIRST LATIN WORDS.
teach.b: Each document is known by its opening words in Latin. Dei Verbum begins with the words for the word of God. Lumen Gentium begins with the light of the nations.
So the name is a doorway: it tells you where the writer chose to start. Then the numbers, and here's the answer to the puzzle.
These documents are divided into short numbered paragraphs, so anyone in any language can point to the same spot.
Say Lumen Gentium 11 in a parish in Lagos or a classroom in Lima, and everyone lands on the same lines, whatever the page.
That's how they'll be read here: one numbered paragraph at a time.

how: Catholics who study Church teaching cite council documents and papal letters by their Latin opening words and paragraph numbers, as in Lumen Gentium 11, and the Vatican publishes them online in many languages.

games.why: a council's constitution, a pope's encyclical, an exhortation: different kinds, different weights, all cited by numbered paragraphs.

practice: If a phone is close, look up Dei Verbum and find the small number one at the start of the first paragraph. Read only that paragraph, slowly, once.
If no phone is near, sit with the two opening words, the word of God, and let them be the doorway into the quiet.
